hook: The Carthaginian general who crossed the Alps with elephants and nearly brought down Rome.

pages.x: Hannibal was born in Carthage in 247 BC, the son of Hamilcar Barca, a general who had fought Rome. When he was nine, his father made him swear at an altar that he would never be a friend of Rome. He grew up in his father's army camps in Spain.

In 218 BC he marched from Spain with about 40,000 men and 37 war elephants, over the Pyrenees, across the Rhone and over the Alps in autumn snow. Cold, rockfalls and mountain tribes cost him nearly half his army, but he came down into Italy, where no one had expected an army to come from.

At Cannae in 216 BC he faced a Roman army almost twice the size of his. He let his centre fall back, then closed his wings and cavalry around the Romans on every side. In one afternoon about 50,000 Romans died. Generals still study Cannae as the perfect battle.

For 15 years he roamed Italy unbeaten. A year before Cannae he had trapped a whole Roman army in the morning fog beside Lake Trasimene. But Rome would not give in, and he never had the siege engines to take it. Roman parents scared their children with the words "Hannibal ad portas!": "Hannibal is at the gates!"

Rome sent Scipio to attack Carthage itself, and Hannibal was called home. At Zama in 202 BC Scipio used Hannibal's own tricks to beat him, and Carthage made peace. When Rome later demanded he be handed over, Hannibal fled east and served foreign kings against Rome.

In 183 BC the Romans finally cornered him in Bithynia, in what is now Turkey. As soldiers surrounded the house, the old general took poison he kept in a ring, saying: "Let us relieve the Romans of the fear they have so long had of an old man."

Hannibal lost his war, and Rome later destroyed Carthage. But he is remembered as one of the greatest generals in history. His march over the Alps and his victory at Cannae are still taught in military academies.
pts: Crossed the Alps with war elephants
Won at Cannae, a model battle for generals ever since
Nearly brought down the Roman Republic
